title: FRESCO: A Novel Consistency Control for Asynchronous Pipeline Parallel Training
claim: Asynchronous updates let parameters change between forward and backward passes, breaking the derivative chain that synchronous execution preserves.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right time, Gantt charts above a parameter-state timeline
description: Two side-by-side Gantt charts, (a) Synchronous and (b) Asynchronous pipeline parallelism, with a time arrow at the top of each. Rows are Stages 1–4 and cells are numbered micro-batches. Blue cells are forward passes, pink cells are backward passes, and hatched gray cells are idle. Green bars mark parameter updates. Micro-batch 3 is outlined in bold with darker fill so it can be tracked through the pipeline. Under each chart is a zoomed Stage 1 row with a parameter-state line. A dashed arc runs from the forward read of micro-batch 3 to its backward pass. In (a) the parameters stay at w. In (b) the parameters move through intermediate states (square, diamond, w+) and a black X marks the mismatch. A legend sits at the right: Forward, Backward, Idle, Update.
caption: Gantt charts illustrating stage-processor states over time for micro-batch pipelining under synchronous and asynchronous parameter updates. Asynchronous updating allows the stage-1 threads for micro-batches 1 and 2 to overwrite the parameters while micro-batch 3 is still waiting on its downstream error signal $\bullet$ after reading the previous parameter state $\bullet$, thus the updated parameters $\blackdiamond$ no longer form a proper derivative chain, degrading its utility for improving stage 1.
abstract: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism can accelerate distributed model training, but suffers from instability caused by inconsistent gradient computations. We identify a fundamental source of this inconsistency: error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not just parameter states. This means that parameters may evolve as long as they preserve forward-equivalence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce FRESCO, which frames asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem: it finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. We demonstrate that FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the gains most pronounced under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels: at pipeline depth 32, it reaches the same loss as the strongest baseline with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8~921$\times$ less memory overhead. Moving beyond the current limitations, FRESCO establishes a new foundation for high-utilization pipeline parallel training, providing a scalable path for large-model development on diverse, resource-constrained systems.
